name: Roto
workload: Generate 10,000 random 8-23 character strings wrapped in Rust userdata objects, then quicksort them in the script using a Rust-implemented comparison (criterion 'Sort Rust objects', one bench() call per iteration).
claimed_speedup: 12.04 ms vs 15.47 ms for Lua 5.5 (mlua) and 36.38 ms for QuickJS (rquickjs) on Sort Rust objects (about 1.3x and 3.0x faster, derived from page data); Koto 49.33 ms, Boa 79.99 ms, Rhai 112.02 ms in the same chart. Slower than Luau (11.82 ms), Wasmi (7.04 ms) and Wasmtime (2.71 ms).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.99.0; cargo criterion with [profile.bench] opt-level=3, lto="fat", codegen-units=1 (Cargo.toml); criterion sample_size 10; mlua Lua 5.5 vendored build, rquickjs 0.14.0; roto 0.12.0 with default-features=false
hardware: Apple M5 Max, macOS 27.0 (README Environment table)
stars_or_usage: 558 stars on the GitHub mirror (project moved to Codeberg; described as used by Rotonda)
tradeoffs: Statically typed, compiled embedded language for Rust hosts, not Lua- or JS-compatible, so existing scripts cannot be reused. Rust-only embedding API. Commit log shows a Cranelift upgrade to fix panics on x86_64, so the JIT back end is still moving.
caveats: Single benchmark (Sort Rust objects), dominated by script-to-Rust interop rather than pure interpreter speed. The numbers exist only in the chart image 'Sort Rust objects.png' in the README, not in text (read from the image). Per-language scripts are hand-written ports (the Lua script uses the userdata < metamethod, the JS script a .lt() method). Hardware is an Apple M5 Max laptop; no other CPU tested. The roto README itself makes no performance claim; the evidence comes from the third-party-style shootout repo by the mlua author, which compares against the mlua and rquickjs bindings rather than standalone C Lua or QuickJS.
found_via: WebSearch 'embeddable scripting language faster than Lua benchmark github' -> khvzak/script-bench-rs; roto row read from its Sort Rust objects.png

name: Lua-CSharp
baseline: NLua (C# binding to native Lua) and MoonSharp (Lua interpreter in C#)
workload: Calling a C# function from Lua 25,000 times (host-call overhead), time and managed allocation.
claimed_speedup: 8.05 ms vs NLua 36.45 ms and MoonSharp 19.87 ms (about 4.5x and 2.5x faster, derived from page data); allocation 31.3 KB vs NLua 12,306.5 KB and MoonSharp 13,887 KB.
tradeoffs: Pure managed C# implementation (works in AOT and Unity, no native dependency, no IL generation) but not every Lua standard library function is supported (see its Compatibility section); strings are UTF-16.
caveats: The README only shows a chart image (docs/Benchmark.png) with no CPU, runtime version or build configuration, and the benchmark source is not linked from the README (repo has a sandbox/ directory only). The workload measures interop call overhead, not Lua execution speed; NLua is the native Lua VM, so this says nothing about Lua-CSharp's VM versus PUC Lua. First-party numbers.
found_via: WebSearch 'C# .NET Lua interpreter or JavaScript engine benchmark faster than MoonSharp NLua Jint github'

name: zig-js
baseline: JavaScriptCore (system framework on macOS, public C embedding API)
workload: Ten small project-owned JavaScript kernels from bench/comparison.js (arithmetic, properties, polymorphic_properties, object_churn, arrays, direct_calls, method_calls, closure_calls, arguments_calls, fibonacci), identical bytes run in both engines with equal-work checksums, seven samples, 50 ms timing floor, alternating runner order.
claimed_speedup: zig-js / JSC throughput 2.32x for a single warmed context (10 of 10 workloads won), 2.53x with 8 independent steady contexts, 2.52x for 8 cold lifecycles; geometric mean JSC single-context throughput is 0.43x zig-js; per-row JSC/zig-js ratio ranges from 0.19x (fibonacci) to 0.82x (object_churn).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.17.0-dev.1441+d5181a9c9, zig-js built ReleaseFast, precise GC enabled; JSC is the macOS system framework 22625.1.24.11.2 with unstated JIT configuration
hardware: Apple M3 Pro, 11 cores, 18 GiB, macOS 27.0, AC power, no CPU pinning
tradeoffs: Exports JavaScriptCore-shaped C headers, so it targets JSC API compatibility; APIs are pre-stabilization; the macOS comparison needs the system JSC framework. Passes 53,175/53,175 configured test262 tests per its README.
caveats: The report itself says the ten kernels 'deliberately exercise guarded native/VM tiers that zig-js currently implements' and is 'not a claim about applications or unsupported workloads'. Beating a production JIT engine by 2-5x on fibonacci and arithmetic is surprising and probably reflects the narrow kernels and an unstated JSC JIT setting through the public C API. The README's own JSON/JIT pipeline diagnostic shows JSC 4.05x faster with no parity claim. README diagnostics name an Apple M2 Pro while the headline report names an M3 Pro. No QuickJS, Duktape or Lua comparison. Project is very new and commits are very frequent.
found_via: WebSearch 'new JavaScript engine written in Rust OR Zig OR Go bytecode VM benchmark results vs QuickJS Boa github 2026' -> zig-utils/zig-js

name: Pipa (pipa-js)
workload: V8 benchmark suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run by the pipa, QuickJS (qjs), Node and Boa binaries, dated 2026-06-15 in the README.
claimed_speedup: README says 'outperforms QuickJS in benchmarks', but its own table shows total score 1075 vs qjs 1101 (-2.4%). Faster than qjs on RegExp (841 vs 306, +174.8%) and NavierStokes (2087 vs 1759, +18.6%); slower on RayTrace (589 vs 1268), EarleyBoyer (1225 vs 1831), Splay (2000 vs 2206), Richards, DeltaBlue and Crypto.
tradeoffs: Pure Rust register VM, about 5.2 MB binary, no C dependencies, embeddable as the pipa-js crate. Partial ES2023: README test262 table shows Proxy 0%, Promise 5.6%, Set 18.8%, Map 22.2%, RegExp 42.3%.
caveats: Headline claim contradicts the README's own overall score (slightly slower than QuickJS); the win is confined to RegExp and NavierStokes. No CPU, flags or QuickJS version stated. A search snippet of an earlier announcement quoted 1256 vs 1219 (not on the page opened, so not used). Added mainly as a regex-engine data point; low conformance weakens the RegExp comparison.
found_via: WebSearch 'new JavaScript engine written in Rust OR Zig OR Go ... beating QuickJS' -> dev.to post (blocked) -> restsend/pipa

name: zig-mquickjs
baseline: MicroQuickJS (bellard/mquickjs, the original C implementation it was ported from)
workload: Octane suite (zig build octane) and a microbenchmark (zig build microbench) run on the same machine for the C original and the Zig port.
claimed_speedup: Octane score 2586 vs 2418 for original mquickjs (higher is better; about +7%, derived from page data); microbench 3603 ns per operation vs 4248 (about 15% less time, derived).
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; build flags of the C original not stated
tradeoffs: Memory-safe-ish Zig port of MicroQuickJS, but the README says it was ported almost entirely by AI and warns 'Do NOT use this if you need anything stable or secure'. Semantics diverge: eval always runs in global scope, let and const act as var; test262 pass rate stated as 18.8% (8,521 of 45,308).
caveats: README states both scores 'move around with CPU load'; CPU model and C build flags unstated; single run pair. Speed gains may come partly from dropped or altered semantics (see test262 rate). Listed as a flagged data point: a Zig rewrite beating a hand-tuned C engine by single-digit percent.
found_via: WebSearch 'new JavaScript engine written in Rust OR Zig OR Go bytecode VM benchmark results vs QuickJS Boa github 2026'

name: Prolua
workload: Twelve scripts in test/bench (binarytrees, closures, coroutines, fannkuch, fib, json, loops, nbody, sort, spectralnorm, strings, tables), whole-process wall time, best of three runs, prolua bench vs the installed lua 5.4.8, measured 2026-09-12.
claimed_speedup: Between 0.60x and 1.19x of the C interpreter's time: faster on sort (0.250 s vs 0.418 s, 0.60x), loops (0.375 s vs 0.521 s, 0.72x), coroutines (0.158 s vs 0.192 s, 0.82x) and nbody (0.612 s vs 0.686 s, 0.89x); parity (1.00-1.03x) on binarytrees, closures, fannkuch, fib, tables; slower on json (1.15x), spectralnorm (1.19x) and strings (1.19x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build bench -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; flags and build of the 'installed' Lua 5.4.8 not stated
tradeoffs: Lua 5.4 reimplementation in Zig with 8-byte NaN-boxed values and 24-byte table nodes; passes the official Lua 5.4.8 suite (30 of 30 runnable files) and byte-for-byte differential tests. Zig package API mirrors the C API shape but is not the C ABI, so existing C hosts cannot link it as liblua.
caveats: Mixed result: wins on 4 of 12 scripts, loses on 3, ties on 5. Whole-process times include startup. CPU model not given (only 'Linux'); the reference Lua is a distro or Homebrew-style install whose build flags are unknown, which can favour either side. Repository is days old (initial release 2026-09-16, three commits).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/lua-vm -> matt-dunleavy/prolua README

name: Cynic
workload: Cross-engine snapshot bench-cross-results.md captured 2026-08-06: interpreter-tier micro fixtures and the vendored Octane compute-six macros, subprocess wall clock, median of N=12 after one warmup, pinned to CPU 1 with taskset, Cynic run with --no-jit (all other JIT engines run JIT-disabled).
claimed_speedup: Micro (ms, Cynic vs qjs): arith_loop 77 vs 369, mod_loop 60 vs 388, array_literal_loop 308 vs 1361, construct_loop 312 vs 977, json_stringify 40 vs 146, class_instantiate 55 vs 173; faster on all 18 micro fixtures where qjs completed (qjs errors on tail_recursion), with near-ties on promise_chain (27 vs 28) and shallow_cons_miss (155 vs 158). Macro: crypto 387 vs 671, splay 479 vs 817, navier-stokes 270 vs 334, raytrace 216 vs 261, richards 579 vs 585 (tie), deltablue 430 vs 344 (slower).
compiler_and_flags: Cynic revision 6e125807, ReleaseFast runner (tools/bench-cross.sh); qjs build flags not stated
hardware: Linux 6.8.0-136-generic x86_64 (CPU model not stated), taskset CPU 1
tradeoffs: Strict-only ECMAScript engine (no sloppy mode, no Annex B, no web-compat built-ins) in Zig with built-in hardening and WebAssembly. Peak RSS is about 3-4x QuickJS in the same snapshot (about 6,000 KiB vs 1,792 KiB on arith_loop).
caveats: The file calls itself an 'internal regression compass - not published', host-local and not comparable across hosts; CPU model missing, so tier C. The comparison is interpreter tier only; in the full-speed table (JIT on) Cynic is roughly 3-12x slower than the fastest of V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore on every macro fixture (that table has no qjs row). Micro fixtures are chosen by the author and several Cynic cells carry >10% spread. README makes no comparative claim.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/javascript-engine?l=zig -> chicoxyzzy/cynic -> docs/benchmarking.md -> bench-cross-results.md

name: uGO
baseline: Tengo, go-lua, GopherLua and goja (Go-embedded scripting engines); native Lua is faster than uGO in the same table
workload: Recursive fib(35) and a tail-recursive fibt(35) in the author's ugobenchfib harness, one run per engine, results dated 2022-05-03 for uGO 0.2.0 release candidate.
claimed_speedup: fib(35): uGO 1.984686 s vs Tengo 2.185415 s, go-lua 2.898563 s, GopherLua 3.211634 s, goja 3.326141 s, starlark-go 4.726492 s (Go 1.18). Native Lua 1.000147 s is about 2x faster than uGO; on fibt(35) uGO 1.261 ms is slower than Tengo 1.135 ms and go-lua 1.006 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.18 (also Go 1.17 table); no extra flags
hardware: Apple M1 host, Parallels VM, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Bytecode stack VM in pure Go, inspired by Tengo (code includes Tengo's BSD-3-Clause/MIT parts), so no cgo; dynamic typing with Go interop. Roughly half the speed of native Lua on fib.
caveats: Does not beat Lua, the named baseline; the win is only over other Go scripting engines. Numbers are from 2022 on uGO 0.2.0-rc, the project is now at v0.5.0, and the table is a single-run fib micro-benchmark run by the author. Mainly useful as a Go-ecosystem data point.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/embedded-language -> ozanh/ugo -> ozanh/ugobenchfib

name: Wasmi (script-bench-rs evidence)
workload: Generate 10,000 random 8-23 character strings wrapped in Rust userdata objects, then quicksort them in the script using a Rust-implemented comparison (criterion 'Sort Rust objects', one bench() call per iteration).
claimed_speedup: 7.04 ms vs 15.47 ms for Lua 5.5 (mlua) and 36.38 ms for QuickJS (rquickjs) on Sort Rust objects (about 2.2x and 5.2x faster, derived from page data); wasmi 2.0.0.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.99.0; cargo criterion with [profile.bench] opt-level=3, lto="fat", codegen-units=1 (Cargo.toml); criterion sample_size 10; mlua Lua 5.5 vendored build, rquickjs 0.14.0; wasmi 2.0.0; wasm module built with rustc -O --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -Cpanic=abort
hardware: Apple M5 Max, macOS 27.0 (README Environment table)
tradeoffs: WebAssembly interpreter: scripts must be compiled to wasm (here Rust compiled with rustc --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -Cpanic=abort -O), so it is not a drop-in scripting language; deterministic, fuel-metered, suited to plug-in sandboxes.
caveats: Single benchmark (Sort Rust objects), dominated by script-to-Rust interop rather than pure interpreter speed. The numbers exist only in the chart image 'Sort Rust objects.png' in the README, not in text (read from the image). Per-language scripts are hand-written ports (the Lua script uses the userdata < metamethod, the JS script a .lt() method). Hardware is an Apple M5 Max laptop; no other CPU tested. The wasmi side runs ahead-of-time compiled Rust (scripts/sort_userdata.wasm.rs), not an interpreted script, so the comparison favours compiled code over Lua and QuickJS sources; wasmi 2.0.0.
found_via: WebSearch 'embeddable scripting language faster than Lua benchmark github' -> khvzak/script-bench-rs

hardware: Apple M5 Max, macOS 27.0 (README Environment table)
tradeoffs: Cranelift-compiled WebAssembly runtime: scripts must be compiled to wasm; large dependency tree compared with a Lua or QuickJS interpreter.
caveats: Single benchmark (Sort Rust objects), dominated by script-to-Rust interop rather than pure interpreter speed. The numbers exist only in the chart image 'Sort Rust objects.png' in the README, not in text (read from the image). Per-language scripts are hand-written ports (the Lua script uses the userdata < metamethod, the JS script a .lt() method). Hardware is an Apple M5 Max laptop; no other CPU tested. The wasmtime side runs ahead-of-time compiled Rust through a JIT, not an interpreted script, so the gap to Lua and QuickJS mostly reflects compiled versus interpreted code.

Luau runs through mlua's luau-jit feature (native code generation enabled), and the Luau script differs slightly from the Lua 5.5 script (table.create).
